text: Raj, a cook, was driving to the market before dawn with a truck full of empty cans. The radio was noisy, so he spoke up. "Hey assistant, how long will it take to get to Fulton Market if I leave tomorrow at five?" The assistant understood that he wanted the drive time to Fulton Market for a five o'clock start the next morning. It checked the roads and said the drive would take about twenty-five minutes, because there was very little traffic that early. Raj also asked it to convert the distance into miles, since the sign he remembered was in kilometers. The assistant said the market was about nine miles away. Raj thanked it, asked it to wake him at four thirty, and went back to loading the cans into the truck.

Marta, an office worker, sat at her desk during lunch and spoke to her phone. "Find me a hotel in Lisbon for three nights. I don't want a room on the street side, it's too loud there." She was dreaming of a sunny week away with her honey, and she hoped the hotel had a pool so they could swim every morning. The assistant understood that she needed a hotel in Lisbon, three nights, two guests, and a quiet room that did not face the street. It found a small hotel with a pool and a room at the back, and it booked the room for her. Then it told her that check-in starts at three o'clock. Marta smiled and went back to her spreadsheet.

When you order food to your home, the app shows a price, a delivery time and a place to leave a tip. People often change a few things before they order. They change the address, the tip, or the time. Many say, "Leave it at the door" or "Bring it up to the third floor." A label on the bag tells the driver which order is yours. If the food is late, people feel sad, so the app shows where the driver is on a map. To change the tip, people say, "Make the tip bigger" or "Tip two dollars." To change the time, they say, "Bring it later" or "Deliver it at six."

Tyre pressure is how much air is inside each tyre. Too little air wears out the tyres and wastes fuel, so it is a serious thing to check. For a new driver it can feel like a puzzle, but it is simple. A gauge shows a number, and a sticker inside the car door shows the right number. If the tyre is low, people ask their assistant or the pump to put more air in. They say, "A little more air in the front tyres," or "Let some air out, it's too hard." After a long trip, a careful driver might celebrate by checking all four tyres once more.

Leo, an office worker, had a video appointment with his doctor at four. He was walking down the street to the office when he spoke to his phone. "When the doctor joins, unmute me, but don't turn my camera on. I'm outside and I don't want her to see the traffic." The assistant understood that he wanted his microphone on and his camera off. At four o'clock it joined the call, unmuted his microphone, and kept the camera off. The call was smooth. Leo explained his headache, the doctor asked a few questions, and the assistant put a reminder on his calendar for a check-up next month.

When you stay at a hotel, you book a room for a number of nights and tell them how many guests are coming. Check-in is usually in the afternoon, and check-out is in the morning. People often change the dates, the number of guests, or the kind of room. They say, "One more night," "Make it for three people," or "Can I have a room on a higher floor?" Most rooms have a kettle to boil water for tea, and if you are hungry late at night, you can ask the front desk about a snack. Staying an extra hour after check-out is also something people ask for.

Nadia had just moved to the city, and it was a cool day in autumn. In her small kitchen she opened the fridge, which was almost empty, and said, "Shopping list." The assistant understood that she wanted to see her shopping list, and it read out the items: bread, eggs and rice. Nadia wanted to enjoy a proper breakfast, so she said, "Gold apples." The assistant understood that she wanted gold apples added to the list, and it put them at the bottom. Then it asked if she would like to find the nearest store. Nadia said yes, and the assistant gave her a short walking route to a market two streets away.

The power went out in Hana's shop just before closing. She owned the little bakery on the corner, and customers were still inside. "Assistant, how long will this power cut last? Is it going to be more than an hour?" The assistant understood that she wanted to know the length of the outage. It checked the power company's page and said that the power should be back in about two hours, which was longer than she hoped. Hana wrote a note with a pencil and taped it to the door. She asked the assistant to text her two workers that they could go home early. She felt proud of how calmly everyone helped carry the bread to the back.

A meal plan is a list of what you will eat during the week. It helps you shop once, waste less food, and avoid the question of what to cook every night. People sort their meals by day, so Monday might be pasta and Tuesday might be soup. When someone is sick, or a friend comes over, they change the plan. They say, "Move the soup to Thursday," "Something light for tonight," or "No meat on Friday." For packed lunches, they ask for easy things, like "Sandwiches for the kids, three days." A good plan is simple and easy to change.

Tom was in a hurry. He was pushing a cart through the outdoor store, zooming past the tents, when he spoke to his phone. "What's the weather on the trail on Saturday? No wait, Sunday. We're leaving Sunday." The assistant understood that Tom had changed his mind and wanted the Sunday forecast. It looked at the most recent forecast for the hills and said it would be cloudy with a light rain after noon. Tom asked for a packing list for a day hike in the rain. The assistant made one: a jacket, water, a map, snacks and dry socks. Tom put a rain jacket in the cart and hurried to the checkout.

Person: Show me how much power I used last week and tell me which hours cost the most.
Assistant: I can do that. Which meter should I look at, the kitchen one or the whole house?
Person: The whole house. The meter is a short distance from my door, in the hall.
Assistant: Last week you used 84 units. The most expensive hours were six to nine at night.
Person: Should I push a button on the meter to save power?
Assistant: No, that won't help. Running the washer in the day will. The sky is clear this week, so solar would work well too.

Ana had just moved to the city, and she was in a small cafe on a rainy afternoon. She had a stale cookie and a good book, and she wanted to spend the afternoon reading. She said to her phone, "Resume book." The assistant understood that she wanted to continue her audiobook, and it started it at chapter nine, right where she had stopped. A few minutes later she asked, "Time left?" The assistant said the chapter had twenty minutes to go, and the whole book was about four hours long. Ana smiled and said, "Bookmark here." The assistant saved the spot.

Mia was seven, and the house felt cold. Her dad, the cook of the family, was busy making soup in the kitchen, so she went to the hall and said to the speaker, "I'm cold. Make it twenty-one degrees, please." The assistant understood that she wanted the heating set to twenty-one degrees. It said, "Okay, the heating is now set to twenty-one." Mia then asked it not to break the quiet rules her dad made about the night, so she said, "Only for tonight, not forever." The assistant understood the change was not permanent, and it said it would go back to the normal setting in the morning.

Lucia, a cook, was making a big dinner for a guest from Brazil, who had flown thousands of kilometers to see her. Her hands were covered in flour, so she typed fast on her phone with one finger: "how do you say welcom in portuguese". The assistant understood the small typo and answered, "Welcome in Portuguese is bem-vindo." It also showed her how to say it out loud. She wanted to sing a plain welcome song at the door, so she asked, "can you spell that slower". The assistant spelled it letter by letter. When the guest arrived, Lucia said it with a big smile.

Priya was in a hurry. Her car engine had been making a strange noise, and she needed money in her account to pay the repair shop before it closed. She felt nervous. Standing at the bus stop, she typed in a rush: "move 200 from savings to checkng". The assistant understood that she wanted two hundred dollars moved from her savings account to her checking account, both her own. It moved the money and told her the new balances. Then she asked it to load her transit card with ten dollars, and the assistant did that too. Her bus arrived, and she got on with a little less worry.

A contact is a small card in your phone with a person's name, phone number, address and birthday. It lets you call or write to someone without remembering the number. Contacts lie in a list, in alphabetical order, so they are easy to find. People change them when someone moves or gets a new number. They say, "Change Dan's number to this one," or "Add a birthday for Aunt Rosa." Some cards have a home number and a back office number. Before saving a number on a card, many people first write it on a note stuck to the microwave.

Sam, a driver, was sitting in his truck outside the diner, looking at the gray sky. He was wearing only jeans and a thin shirt, and the wind was making the truck rock. "Wow, it looks cold out there," he said to the assistant. "I wonder if I need my coat for the wide road over the hills." The assistant understood that he was asking about the weather. It said that the temperature outside was four degrees, with rain coming after lunch. It suggested a warm coat. Sam went inside to eat the soup that the diner would serve, and then he took his coat from the back seat.

Dana, a busy parent, was mopping the kitchen floor while her kids worked on a craft project in the living room. The electric bill had come that morning, and it was higher than normal. "It feels like the lights are on all day," she said to the assistant. "And the kids always forget the heater in their room." The assistant understood that she wanted to save power. It turned off the lights in three empty rooms and switched off the heater in the kids' room. Then it told her which rooms used the most power this week. Dana thanked it and went back to her mopping.

Ben was a student, and moving day had finally come. His room was full of dirty boxes and rolls of tape that he got at the shop on the corner. He was worried about the movers, so he asked his phone, "Movers time?" The assistant understood that he wanted to know when the movers would arrive. It checked his calendar and said they were coming at ten, in about two hours. Ben said, "Boxes list." The assistant read out the list of boxes he had made: books, kitchen, clothes and desk. Ben marked the last box as packed and sat down to wait.

Grandpa Joe was planning a trip to see his sister. He sat in his car in the driveway and said, "Assistant, I mixed up the exits last time. Is there a way to get there with fewer turns? And less time than before?" The assistant understood that he wanted a simpler route that was shorter than his old one. It found a road with only four turns, and said it would take about ten minutes less. Joe asked it to read the directions slowly, one step at a time. The assistant said the first step: stay on Main Street for half a mile. Joe nodded and backed out of the driveway.

Elena, a nurse after a night shift, came home tired and went straight to the kitchen. She needed more coffee than usual, so she said to the coffee machine, "Make it double strength, and give me two cups." The assistant understood that she wanted the coffee twice as strong, with two cups instead of one. While it brewed, she turned on some music. A text came in with an urgent note from the hospital, asking if she could work an extra hour tomorrow. She rounded the counter and asked the assistant to reply yes. It sent the message, and the machine beeped. Elena drank her coffee and finally sat down.

Air in a home can get dry, dusty or stale. A purifier cleans the air by pulling it through a filter, and a humidifier adds a little water to dry air. Opening a window brings in fresh air. Bad air can be a serious problem for people with allergies. People change the speed, the room, and the time. They say, "Turn the purifier up," "Run it on low tonight," or "Make the air less dry." Most machines have a light that changes color when the air is dirty. It is good to read the note on the filter and change it when it gets gray.

Henry, a gardener, was done watering the roses and had a little time before a shower. He stepped out onto the path and said to his watch, "Tell me how many steps I took today." The assistant understood that he wanted the step count. It said he had walked six thousand steps, about four kilometers. Henry wanted to reach ten thousand, so he asked it to remind him every hour to walk. Then he said, "Start a walk, twenty-five minutes." The assistant began timing the walk and told him he was keeping a good pace. Henry walked around the park until the timer rang.
